title: Maximum and Minimum of Independent Variables
short: P(max ≤ x) = F(x)ⁿ and P(min > x) = (1 − F(x))ⁿ; the minimum of independent exponential variables is exponential with the rates added.
trouble: Students write P(max ≤ x) as n · F(x), or try to find P(min ≤ x) directly instead of through its complement.

blocks.html: A system of parts in series fails when its first part fails; a job finishes when its slowest worker does. These are the minimum and the maximum of several random variables. With independence and CDFs both have neat formulas, and the minimum of exponential times is exponential again.

For independent $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ with the same CDF $F$: $$P(\max \le x) = F(x)^{n}, \qquad P(\min > x) = (1 - F(x))^{n}.$$ If the $X_i$ are exponential with rates $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$, the minimum is exponential with rate $\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n$, and $X_i$ is the first with probability $\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n}$.

The largest is at most $x$ exactly when every $X_i$ is at most $x$; by independence, the probabilities multiply. Likewise the smallest exceeds $x$ exactly when every $X_i$ does. For exponentials, $$P(\min > t) = \prod e^{-\lambda_i t} = e^{-(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n)t}$$ Working through these "all of them" statements avoids the hard "at least one" cases.

blocks.name: prob-region
blocks.cap: Two independent uniform numbers: the larger is below 0.6 exactly when the point lies in the small square, whose area is 0.6 squared.

blocks.title: Dice
blocks.q: Roll 3 dice. Find the probability that the largest is at most 4, and that it is exactly 4.

blocks.title: The largest of n uniforms
blocks.q: $n$ numbers are uniform on $[0, 1]$, independent. Find the expected largest.
steps: $F_{\max}(x) = x^{n}$, so the density is $nx^{n - 1}$ on $[0, 1]$.
The $n$ points split $[0, 1]$ into $n + 1$ gaps of equal average length.

blocks.title: Parts in series
blocks.q: A device has two parts with independent exponential lifetimes, means 4 years and 12 years, and fails when either part fails. Find its mean lifetime and the chance that the first part fails first.
steps: The device's lifetime is exponential with rate $\frac{1}{3}$: mean 3 years.
The first part fails first with probability $\frac{1/4}{1/3} = \frac{3}{4}$.

blocks.html: The exponential case has a memorable form. Think of independent alarm clocks ringing at exponential times. The first ring comes at rate $\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n$, so the chance that all of them are still silent at time $t$ is $e^{-(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n)t}$, and clock $i$ rings first with probability equal to its share of the total rate. After the first ring the others start fresh, because exponentials have no memory.

Writing $P(\max \le x) = n \cdot F(x)$ (which can exceed 1), or attacking $P(\min \le x)$ directly, which needs inclusion–exclusion. Check: rewrite the event about the max or min as "all of them" and multiply; for the min, use the complement: $P(\min \le x) = 1 - (1 - F(x))^{n}$.
